strengths: Technically solid and clearly written extension of the CCDB framework: the fine-grained distribution matching (FG-CCDB) is derived cleanly, and closed-form group-level reweighting (Equations 2-4) is simple, efficient, and requires no iterative optimization.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: five benchmarks spanning binary (Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments) and multi-class (cMNIST, cCIFAR10) settings with varying bias-conflicting ratios, 5 random seeds, and comparisons against both bias-supervised and bias-agnostic baselines.

Well-designed ablations: the paper isolates the contribution of BEO (GroupDRO-BEO, DFR-BEO) and FG-CCDB (FG-CCDB-sup), showing BEO predictions are a strong proxy for human annotations, and analyzes the effect of repeating the bias enhancement stage.
Strong empirical results in highly biased multi-class settings (cMNIST/cCIFAR10), where FG-CCDB clearly outperforms existing bias-agnostic methods and even bias-supervised baselines.
Honest discussion of limitations (cases where group imbalance deviates from the one-majority-bias-per-class pattern), plus supplementary details on hyperparameters and sample weight distributions.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. BEO is essentially a combination of well-established ideas: overfitting-based identification of minority/bias-conflicting samples (JTT, LfF, SELF, DPR) plus a top-50% confidence data-selection amplification step. FG-CCDB is an incremental refinement of CCDB that replaces single-Gaussian matching with quantized group-level matching; both components build heavily on prior work with relatively modest methodological innovation.

Restrictive structural assumption |Y| = |S| (one abstract bias attribute per class) substantially limits generality. Since pseudo-bias labels are produced by a class-biased model, group prediction largely reduces to predicting class labels of an overfitted model, which may not capture datasets with multiple or heterogeneous bias attributes per class; this limitation is acknowledged but not explored experimentally.

The most convincing gains are on synthetic datasets (cMNIST, cCIFAR10); on real-world binary benchmarks the improvement over CCDB is marginal (e.g., Waterbirds worst-group 90.56 vs 90.48), so the real-world impact of the fine-grained component is less clearly demonstrated.

Model selection criterion is ambiguous: the best model is chosen by 'highest worst-class accuracy on the validation set,' but it is unclear whether this requires group/bias annotations on the validation set, which would weaken the claimed fully bias-agnostic positioning (the paper emphasizes no annotations during 'training or validation').

Table 3 reports only i.i.d. accuracy (not worst-group) for FG-CCDB rows on cMNIST/cCIFAR10, an inconsistent and incomplete comparison with the supervised variants; some reported std. deviations (e.g., ±0.005, ±0.001) appear implausible or mislabeled.

Scalability of the closed-form weighting relies on the number of groups equaling C×C; behavior when BEO's group predictions are noisy or when groups are near-empty (small Ni,j producing extreme weights) is not analyzed or safeguarded.

The key baseline CCDB [19] is itself an arXiv preprint, so the work builds on and extends a non-peer-reviewed method; positioning relative to the newest bias-discovery literature (e.g., recent CLIP-based or language-based bias explorers) is somewhat thin.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation across five benchmarks (real-world binary: Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments; synthetic multi-class: cMNIST, cCIFAR10) with multiple bias-conflicting ratios and 5 random seeds, which is above average rigor for this area
The closed-form group reweighting (Eqs. 2-4) is simple, efficient, and avoids the iterative optimization and per-sample feature storage required by CCDB; the efficiency argument is convincing

The ablation is well designed: replacing ground-truth annotations with BEO predictions in GroupDRO/DFR (GroupDRO-BEO, DFR-BEO) directly tests the claim that BEO is a viable substitute for human bias labels, and FG-CCDB-sup isolates the contribution of the reweighting scheme itself

The paper is generally readable, positions itself against a broad taxonomy of related work (bias exploration vs. mitigation, annotation-dependent vs. agnostic), and honestly acknowledges limitations in the conclusion (e.g., failure modes when group imbalance deviates from the assumed pattern)
Strong worst-group results in highly biased multi-class settings (Table 2), where the method clearly outperforms both bias-supervised and bias-agnostic baselines
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The core idea is a quantized/discretized variant of CCDB combined with pseudo-bias labels from an overfitted model - both ingredients are well established (CCDB [19], JTT/SELF/LfF-style overfitting-based bias identification, GEORGE-style subgroup partitioning). Equations 2-4 are essentially contingency-table normalization, not a new statistical framework; the framing as a 'mixture of latent groups' is overstated, since distributions are only discretized along a single bias dimension rather than actually modeled as mixtures in feature space

Restrictive assumptions that undermine generality: the method assumes |Y| = |S| and that each class is spuriously correlated with a single abstract bias attribute. All five benchmarks satisfy this by construction, and the paper concedes that settings violating this (e.g., multiple bias attributes, asymmetric group structures like CivilComments) weaken the overfitting signal. The method's applicability to realistic multi-bias scenarios is therefore untested

Heavy reliance on CCDB [19], which is itself an unpublished arXiv preprint (arXiv:2504.17314). Building the entire contribution on a non-peer-reviewed baseline makes it difficult to assess the true delta over established literature, and GEORGE-style clustering baselines are cited but never empirically compared despite being the closest alternative for subgroup discovery

The claimed hyperparameter-free nature is weakened in practice: the method introduces γ = 10%, top-50% confidence selection, the number of 'bias enhancement' repetitions (3), and 20-epoch/5000-iteration schedules, all tuned per benchmark in the appendix

Reporting inconsistencies raise reproducibility concerns: Table 3 reports std devs as small as ±0.001-0.007 for FG-CCDB on Waterbirds/CelebA, whereas Table 1 reports ±0.24-0.52 for the same configuration; Table 1 also contains single-decimal results mixed with ±std results without explanation. No code release is mentioned

Multiple writing/technical sloppiness issues: typos throughout ('foucus', 'banchmark', 'bia-supervised', 'solved' for 'solves'), a duplicated/circular citation [2]/[15], and imprecise claims (e.g., asserting exact distribution matching while the underlying p(z|y) is still approximated from a biased model's features)

On the flagship real-world benchmarks the gains over the direct baseline CCDB are modest (Waterbirds: 90.48 vs 90.56 worst-group, within noise), with the headline improvements concentrated on synthetic datasets, so the practical significance of the 'fine-grained' extension on real data is only partially demonstrated

strengths: The proposed FG-CCDB is simple, lightweight, and computationally attractive: sample weights are computed in closed form at the group level, avoiding the iterative optimization and per-sample feature storage required by CCDB.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation covering real-world binary benchmarks (Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments) and challenging multi-class settings (cMNIST, cCIFAR10) with multiple bias-conflicting ratios, 5 random seeds, and both bias-supervised and bias-agnostic baselines.

Strong empirical results: FG-CCDB matches or surpasses bias-supervised upper bounds on several datasets, with particularly large gains in highly biased multi-class scenarios, which is a convincing demonstration of practical value.

Good ablation design: BEO is validated as a drop-in replacement for human annotations in GroupDRO/DFR, and FG-CCDB-sup isolates the contribution of fine-grained reweighting from the bias prediction module.
Useful mechanistic analyses (feature-class/bias correlations in Figure 3, sample-weight distributions in Figure 5) that go beyond accuracy tables and support the claimed mechanism.
Honest discussion of limitations in the conclusion (scenarios where a class is not dominated by a single bias attribute).
weaknesses: Limited novelty: BEO is essentially a variant of existing overfitting/exploiting-misclassification approaches (JTT, LfF, SELF, DPR) with a confidence-based top-50% data selection step, and FG-CCDB is a direct refinement of CCDB (itself only an arXiv preprint). The paper's contribution builds almost entirely on one prior work, making the overall advance incremental.

Restrictive modeling assumption: |Y| = |S|, i.e., each class is spuriously correlated with exactly one bias attribute, and the method implicitly assumes a one-to-one class-bias correspondence. Real-world datasets with multiple or shared bias attributes per class (common in practice) fall outside this assumption, and the paper does not empirically test such cases.

Potential inconsistency in the bias-agnostic claim: model selection is based on 'the highest worst-class accuracy on the validation set', which normally requires bias annotations in the validation set. The paper claims no annotations are needed for validation but does not clearly explain how worst-class accuracy is obtained annotation-free, and baselines are characterized as needing validation annotations under seemingly similar protocols.

Suspicious statistics in Table 3: the std. devs. reported for FG-CCDB and FG-CCDB-sup (e.g., ±0.005, ±0.001) are inconsistent with the same methods' variance in Table 1 (±0.52, ±0.24), which undermines confidence in the reported results.

Heavy dependence on the quality of the pseudo-bias predictor: since weights are computed directly from BEO group assignments, systematic errors in bias prediction propagate directly into reweighting; robustness to noisy or missing group structure (e.g., overlapping bias attributes) is not analyzed.

Presentation quality issues: numerous typos ('foucus', 'banchmark', 'bia-supervised', 'leaning'), duplicated references ([2] and [15]), minor grammatical errors, and figure legends (Figure 4) that are hard to read; these suggest the manuscript needed another careful pass.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across six benchmarks (Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments, UrbanCars, cMNIST, cCIFAR10) covering single-shortcut, multi-shortcut, and extreme multi-class bias scenarios, with 5 seeds and standard splits for fair comparison.

The proposed FG-CCDB yields clear and consistent gains over its direct predecessor CCDB, particularly in highly biased multi-class settings (e.g., +5 to +9 points on cMNIST) and multi-shortcut UrbanCars, and compares favorably with bias-supervised methods without requiring annotations.

MST is validated not only through final task accuracy but also directly against ground-truth group annotations (F1/precision/recall in Fig. 4, Table 9), which is more rigorous than most annotation-free debiasing papers; the ablations (GroupDRO-MST, DFR-MST, FG-CCDB-sup) cleanly isolate the contribution of each component.
The method is lightweight and efficient: closed-form mode-level weights avoid CCDB's iterative per-sample optimization, and computational costs are honestly reported (Tables 10-11).
Limitations are candidly acknowledged in the conclusions (failure modes on CelebA and CivilComments), and hyperparameter sensitivity (γ, β) is analyzed with supporting tables.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core recipe (train a biased ERM on a subset, use its predictions as pseudo-bias labels, filter/select high-confidence samples, reweight) is assembled from well-established ideas (JTT, SELF, XRM, Lee et al. 2023, Ciranni et al. 2025); the 'fine-grained' contribution reduces to a closed-form reweighting of confusion-matrix cells, which is a fairly incremental extension of CCDB rather than a new principle.

The restriction that the bias label space shares the label space of the target (|S| = |Y|, s ∈ S predicted by the biased classifier) is a strong and somewhat restrictive assumption that is not deeply analyzed; it is unclear how the method degrades when bias attributes span a different or larger space than the class labels.

Gains on the canonical binary benchmarks are modest: on Waterbirds the WGA improvement over CCDB is within noise (90.56 vs 90.48), and i.i.d. accuracy on CelebA/Waterbirds is slightly below CCDB, so the headline advantage rests mostly on the synthetic multi-class datasets.

The paper assumes hard, binary mode assignments with uniform weighting within each mode; while the authors report that entropy-based intra-mode splitting hurt, the intra-mode homogeneity assumption and the aggressive weight ratios (up to 1000) may be fragile on datasets where a mode contains heterogeneous sub-biases.

Theoretical grounding is thin: the EOF-criterion argument in the appendix is informal (illustrated only by toy matrices), and the claimed equivalence between distribution matching and covariate-balance/causal debiasing (citing only a course-notes reference) is asserted rather than established.

Presentation issues: the appendix retains reviewer-response artifacts (R1W1, R2W2, R3Q1, etc.), several tables lack standard deviations (Tables 1, 2, 4 for baseline entries), and some claims (e.g., 'reliably captures harmful implicit bias cues as long as a < 100%') are stronger than the evidence provided.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning single-shortcut (Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments), multi-shortcut (UrbanCars), and highly biased multi-class benchmarks (cMNIST, cCIFAR10) with 5 random seeds.
The proposed weights have a closed-form solution, making the reweighting step lightweight and scalable compared to CCDB's iterative sample-level optimization.

The ablations are reasonable: MST is used to replace human annotations in GroupDRO and DFR, and FG-CCDB is also evaluated with ground-truth modes (FG-CCDB-sup), which helps isolate the contribution of each module.
The analysis of hyperparameters (gamma, beta) and repetitions, and the analysis of how reweighting shifts feature correlations away from bias (Figure 3), support the main claims.
The paper is candid about limitations (e.g., failure modes on CelebA and CivilComments where the overfitting signal is weak).
weaknesses: Limited novelty over prior work. The core idea is a relatively incremental extension of CCDB (Zhao et al., 2025): replacing a single-Gaussian approximation with a discrete confusion-matrix-based approximation. The MST bias-exploration component largely recombines known ideas (exploiting ERM overfitting, removing bias-conflicting samples, confidence-based selection from Lee et al. 2023, Ciranni et al. 2025, JTT, SELF). The combination is competent but not a significant conceptual advance.

The manuscript is not publication-ready. Appendix E contains leftover rebuttal material addressed to reviewers (R1W1, R2W2, R3W1, etc.), and the main text has numerous grammatical errors (e.g., 'capable of tackling multi-shortcuts by relate the hard confusion matrix', 'exactly correspond to', 'inherently solved', 'with multi-stage refinement, our method achieving'). This indicates poor preparation.

A potentially serious evaluation inconsistency: the paper claims to be fully bias-agnostic, yet model selection uses 'the highest worst-class accuracy on the validation set', which in principle requires group/bias annotations on the validation set. The relation between this selection criterion and the claimed 'Val: No' bias-label setting in Table 1 is not clearly justified.

The assumption that the bias label space has the same size as the class space (|S| = |Y|) is restrictive and only weakly justified; it is unclear how well the mode partition reflects bias structure when the number of genuine bias groups differs substantially from C, or under multiple concurrent shortcuts where the confusion matrix can only encode C bias labels.

The key design choices are heuristic and dataset-dependent: beta = 50% works because bias-aligned ratios exceed ~90% on most benchmarks (CelebA is a near-boundary case at 51.72%), and the extremely aggressive reweighting (weight ratios up to 1000) raises stability concerns that are not analyzed theoretically.

Gains over the CCDB baseline are marginal on Waterbirds (90.56 vs 90.48 WGA) and modest on several other settings, so the central claim of 'significantly outperforming' holds mainly in the highly biased synthetic multi-class scenarios; the real-world evidence is mixed.
Reproducibility is questionable: the 'Code:' placeholder on page 1 is empty, and no code link is provided.

Missing baselines/positioning in places: some compared methods report missing entries, and the comparison with DDB on UrbanCars (which has smaller gaps but lower ID accuracy) is discussed but not convincingly reconciled with the paper's claims of best overall performance.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated extension of the CCDB line of work: replacing the single-Gaussian distribution approximation with a discrete, multi-modal approximation derived from a hard confusion matrix is a sensible fix for a real limitation, and the closed-form reweighting (Eq. 3-4) is lightweight and removes the need for iterative optimization of sample weights.

Comprehensive and convincing empirical evaluation: experiments span binary (Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments), multi-shortcut (UrbanCars), and highly biased multi-class (cMNIST, cCIFAR10) settings, with 5 seeds, standard splits, and comparisons against a broad set of bias-supervised, pseudo-supervised, and bias-agnostic baselines including recent methods (DDB, DaC, GERNE, XRM, uLA).

Strong results in the most relevant regimes: FG-CCDB clearly outperforms CCDB and bias-supervised baselines in multi-class, highly biased settings (e.g., +7-9 points on cMNIST), and the MST-as-annotation-proxy ablation (GroupDRO-MST, DFR-MST) is a nice validation of the bias-exploration module's practical value.

Good transparency about limitations: the authors honestly acknowledge failure modes (CelebA's single minority group, CivilComments patterns) and provide detailed ablations on gamma, beta, repetition count, and computational cost, plus quantitative mode-prediction F1/precision/recall against ground-truth annotations.
The analysis of inferred sample weights (Figure 5) and feature bias/class correlations (Figure 3) provides mechanistic evidence that the reweighting actually reduces reliance on spurious features.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: MST is essentially an iterative variant of well-established bias-amplification ideas (JTT, SELF, Lee et al. 2023, Ciranni et al. 2025 all exploit ERM overfitting and removal/identification of bias-conflicting samples), and FG-CCDB is a fairly direct closed-form refinement of CCDB's objective. In the single-shortcut case, mode-wise reweighting largely collapses to conventional group balancing, and the claimed distinctions from group balancing (Sec. 3.2) are more philosophical than substantive.

Gains on the canonical real-world binary benchmarks are marginal: on Waterbirds WGA improves over CCDB by only 0.08 (90.56 vs 90.48) and i.i.d. accuracy slightly drops; on CelebA i.i.d. drops. The headline improvements come mainly from synthetic multi-class datasets, raising questions about how broadly the fine-grained matching helps in realistic regimes.

The setup relies on assumptions that may not hold in practice: the auxiliary bias model shares the label space (|S|=|Y|), which implicitly ties bias structure to class count; the intra-mode homogeneity assumption is justified only empirically; and the argument that beta=50% works because bias-aligned ratio >50% is an empirical heuristic, not a guarantee.

Model selection uses worst-class accuracy on a validation set, and several of the strongest 'unsupervised' competitors are compared under different validation protocols (some baselines require held-out bias annotations for tuning/model selection), making some cross-method comparisons not perfectly apples-to-apples despite the bias-agnostic claim.

No theoretical analysis of when the multi-stage retraining converges or when the confusion-matrix-based mode partition recovers the true group structure; the EOF-criterion connection in the appendix is informal and only sketched.

Dependence on the quality of a small biased model (10% of data, 20 epochs) introduces a potential brittleness for datasets where ERM does not latch onto a dominant shortcut early, which the authors themselves concede; sensitivity to seed/γ on such datasets is under-explored.

The paper builds very heavily on a single recent baseline (CCDB, itself an arXiv preprint); if that line of work is not broadly established, the contribution should be framed more independently rather than as an incremental 'fine-grained variant'.
